analysis.one_liner: Stops construction of new AI data centers until Congress passes laws protecting workers, consumers, and communities from AI's costs.
analysis.headline: Ten House Democrats introduced a bill to halt construction of new AI data centers until Congress passes AI safety and worker protections; it has been referred to committee and has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would ban the construction or upgrading of large AI data centers starting immediately, and the ban would stay in place until Congress passes laws that: put federal safety review over AI products, protect workers from losing their jobs to automation, share AI's wealth more broadly, and require any new data center to win community approval, avoid raising electric bills, avoid worsening climate change, take no subsidies, and provide union jobs. It would also block exports of the computer chips and hardware used to run AI data centers to countries without comparable laws. It was introduced by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and referred to House committees, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities that would otherwise host large AI data centers gain veto power and public reporting on water, power, emissions, and jobs. Utility customers gain protection from rate increases driven by data center power demand. Workers gain leverage for union wages and protections against AI-driven displacement before new computing capacity is built.

how_it_helps.text: It stops new AI data center construction and upgrades until Congress enacts laws requiring federal safety review of AI products, protection of workers from displacement, and shared economic gains.

For future data centers it would require that they not raise consumers' electricity bills, not worsen climate change, win approval from affected communities, receive no subsidies, and create union jobs with prevailing wages and apprenticeships.

It orders the Energy Department to publish quarterly reports on each data center's water and energy use, emissions, noise, wages, jobs, and any subsidies, and lets the Secretary verify compliance with subpoenas and inspections.
It bars exporting computing hardware for AI use to countries that lack comparable AI laws, aiming to prevent the buildout from simply moving abroad.

analysis.who_pays: Large tech companies and AI developers, who could not build or expand data centers until new laws pass, and businesses and consumers who rely on growing computing capacity.chipmakers and hardware exporters could lose foreign sales under the export controls.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium has no end date of its own: it lifts only if Congress enacts new laws imposing federal pre-release review of AI products, anti-displacement and wealth-sharing policies, and strict per-facility conditions, and if that legislation expressly terminates the moratorium — a bar so high it could function as a permanent ban.

The bill bans construction and upgrading of AI data centers over 20 megawatts outright, which would stop capacity expansion that could otherwise lower the marginal cost of computing and cloud services consumers and businesses use.
The export control section bars selling AI-related computing hardware to any country without comparable AI laws, which could hurt US chip and hardware makers' foreign sales and invite retaliation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and growing cost — AI data centers' enormous electricity, water, and land demands that can raise utility bills and strain local infrastructure — and would give affected communities veto power while requiring union wages and banning subsidies. But the mechanism is extremely blunt: a total construction freeze with no end date certain, contingent on Congress passing sweeping AI safety and wealth-sharing laws that have no realistic path to enactment, and it applies to companies regardless of conduct. An honest supporter would acknowledge that it shuts down data center construction entirely as leverage, and the export control provisions would likely push other countries to build their own supply chains. The cost is forgone infrastructure and investment during the freeze; the benefit is time and leverage to impose safety and cost protections before further buildout.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees in June 2026, and no committee or floor action has followed since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 24, 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Foreign Affairs Committee.
No further action — no hearings, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history after the referrals.
It attracted 17 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 217 House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large tech companies building AI data centers are better off so far, since nothing has slowed or conditioned the buildout; communities facing proposed data centers have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big Tech and AI data center builders

for.name: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a moratorium on new AI data center construction.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee; House Foreign Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and have taken no action on it since.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republicans support the bill, while no opposition votes have occurred yet; the split so far is entirely along party lines.

industries.note: The bill freezes construction and upgrading of AI data centers over 20 megawatts until sweeping new laws pass, halting the physical expansion these companies' AI businesses depend on.

New large data centers are a major source of load growth that can push up electricity bills; the bill would require future facilities not to raise consumer utility bills, while halting new large industrial customers during the moratorium.
The export control section bars selling computing hardware for AI use to countries without comparable AI laws, cutting off some foreign sales.
Communities would gain veto power over future data centers, and consumers would gain protection from electricity bill increases, plus public reporting on water use, emissions, and jobs.

analysis.trajectory: A sweeping bill with a small, all-Democratic cosponsor list that was referred to two committees and has seen no hearings or markup; most bills at this stage never reach a floor vote, and this one is very unlikely to advance in this Congress.
